name: mock
intent: Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts.
problem: The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.
context: Unit and component tests of an object whose collaboration protocol is the specification: exact calls, arguments, cardinality or order matter (handshakes, publish-once, audit logging, cache invalidation) and the collaborator is slow, unavailable, non-deterministic or side-effecting. It requires a substitutable dependency (dependency injection or lookup) and, for framework-based realizations, an interception mechanism - dynamic proxy, bytecode agent, generated code or macro. Typical in mockist, interaction-first TDD and in need-driven development.
benefits: Behaviour verification is the assertion: the expectation is an executable specification, and a missing, unexpected, wrongly-typed or out-of-order call fails the test at the moment it deviates, while the stack and arguments are still available (Meszaros' Mock Object; gMock).
Isolation: the real collaborator's latency, availability and side effects are irrelevant, because only the SUT's outbound protocol is exercised.
Verification logic lives in the double instead of being repeated in every test, which removes the duplication Meszaros calls Test Code Duplication between similar tests.
Non-deterministic and rare paths - timeouts, exceptions, malformed replies - become reproducible: programme the collaborator's failure and assert how the SUT reacts.
The expectation list documents the collaborator's protocol in one readable place, so a change to the interaction contract surfaces as a changed expectation.
Used while designing, expectations written before the implementation expose over-coupled or over-large collaborations early (gMock explicitly presents mocks as a design tool).
tradeoffs: Tests couple to implementation detail: a refactoring that preserves behaviour but changes the call sequence breaks the test, the fragile-test failure Meszaros calls Overspecified Software and Fowler calls coupling tests to implementations.

All expected behaviour must be specified before the SUT is exercised, so tests read unlike ordinary arrange-act-assert tests and are harder to write and read for newcomers (Meszaros' implementation notes on Mock Object).

Expectations encode the test author's assumption about the collaborator's contract; a green mockist test does not prove the real depended-on component honours it, so a double-free contract or integration test remains mandatory.

Interception machinery - dynamic proxies (Moq, Mockito, NSubstitute), bytecode agents (MockK on the JVM), compile-time generators (Cuckoo, mockgen) - costs test-time performance, complicates debugging, and cannot intercept final/sealed types, static members, inline functions or structs.

The strictness dial has two failure modes: overly strict expectations cause spurious failures, while lenient mocks that return null/default values let unstubbed paths pass silently (Moq's Loose behaviour, Mockito's default answers).

Mocking everything turns the suite into a test of its own script; several collaborating mocks assert your expectations rather than the system, which is why test-double usage needs a deliberate boundary.

participants.responsibility: Exercises the collaborator through its normal interface, unaware that it is talking to a double; only its observable behaviour is the point of the test.

Implements the collaborator's interface, compares each received call with the programmed expectations and records fulfilment, failing the test on an unexpected call, a wrong argument or a prohibited order.
The programmed call specification - method, argument matchers, cardinality, sequence position, and the return value or exception - derived from the requirement, not from the current implementation.
Constructs, configures and installs the mock, exercises the SUT, triggers final verification and asserts the SUT's own results.
The substitutable dependency (constructor or setter injection, factory, lookup, test-specific subclass) through which the mock replaces the real collaborator for the duration of the test.

use_cases: Verifying that a component emits exactly the expected messages to a collaborator whose effects are otherwise invisible: an audit logger, notifier, event publisher or payment gateway.
Pinning an interaction protocol whose ordering and cardinality are the requirement - open before send, publish exactly once, flush before close - in tests of clients and adapters.
Simulating failure paths of a remote collaborator (timeout, exception, malformed response) to assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from them deterministically.
Unit-testing a domain service against repository, clock, or gateway interfaces when the real implementations are slow, licensed or unavailable in the development environment.
Driving interface design from the outside in: write the expectation for the call the SUT should make, then let the implementation satisfy it (mockist TDD).
Verifying that a main operation triggers its side effects - cache invalidation, metrics emission, compensating call - with the required arguments.
In C++ tests built with GoogleTest gMock, using EXPECT_CALL matchers, Times cardinalities and InSequence ordering verifies an outbound collaborator protocol before the SUT runs.
In Java tests using Mockito, verify and InOrder assert required interactions with a dependency while keeping the interaction contract separate from the dependency's implementation.
In Python's unittest.mock, assert_called_once_with and assert_has_calls verify argument, cardinality and sequence requirements for calls made through a replaceable collaborator.
avoid_when: The interaction is not the behaviour under test: use a Stub for canned answers or a Fake for a working lightweight implementation; mocks are for when calls, arguments, cardinality or order are the specification (Meszaros' Stub vs Mock distinction).

The collaborator is a value object, a third-party type you do not own, or a trivial data holder - the real thing is cheap and mocking it verifies nothing (Mockito's 'do not mock value objects', 'do not mock types you don't own').
A fast, deterministic in-memory implementation is available: a fake exercises real sequences and avoids interaction coupling.
The behaviour spans several collaborators and only the end-to-end flow matters; a wider test with real or fake components answers the question, while many mocks mostly assert the test's own script.

Legacy code offers no substitutable dependency, or the seam is a final/static member: extract an interface, use a Test-Specific Subclass, or add the seam first - mocking is only as good as the substitution point.
anti_patterns: Mocking the system under test itself, or mocking so much of the collaboration that the test verifies the scripted conversation rather than production behaviour.
Strict expectations on every call, producing Overspecified Software: behaviour-preserving refactorings break tests, and the team reacts by weakening or deleting the assertions.
Verifying what was stubbed - asserting the mock's programmed return value or its own recorded calls instead of the SUT's outcome - which makes the test a tautology.
Mocking by wishful thinking: fabricating a collaborator contract that no double-free test ever checks, so the real integration ships untested.
Asserting order and exact call counts where the requirement does not imply them, encoding incidental sequencing of the current implementation into the suite.
Returning default values from unstubbed calls and treating the resulting green run as coverage of paths that were never exercised.
design_principles: Behaviour verification as a first-class specification mechanism, complementing state verification (Meszaros' Behavior Verification).
Depend on abstractions: the SUT must depend on an interface or replaceable seam before any double can be installed (dependency inversion).
Separate the double's responsibility from the implementation's: the mock verifies one collaborator's protocol, it does not carry business rules.
Precision principle: expect exactly the interactions the requirement implies - no more (avoid overspecification), no fewer (avoid untested protocol).
Test through public interfaces: expectations are written against the collaborator's published interface, never against the SUT's internals.
best_practices: Follow the pattern's fixture sequence: construct the mock, configure the expectations, install it, exercise the SUT, run final verification - configuring after installation is undefined behaviour in frameworks such as gMock.

Keep expectations exactly as strong as the requirement: use argument matchers and cardinality deliberately, constrain order only for calls whose ordering is part of the protocol, and forbid calls the protocol excludes.
Run final verification explicitly (verify(mock), AssertExpectations, confirmVerified, Sequence/checkpoint) so unmet expectations fail the test instead of being forgotten.
Pair every mocked collaborator contract with at least one test against the real implementation or a fake, so the assumed contract is validated.
Mock only types you own or wrap first: introduce an interface you control around third-party, final or sealed dependencies.
Reset or recreate mocks per test, and name the mock and each expectation after the requirement it encodes, so failures read as requirement violations.
When several tests need the same collaborator role, factor the programmed double into a configurable test double or fixture rather than copying expectation blocks.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code, Chapter 23 'Test Double Patterns' - Mock Object (p. 544) and Test Double (p. 522), Addison-Wesley 2007.
